questions.explain: The chapter splits forecasting into univariate time-series (seasonal infrastructure metrics like CPU, connections, I/O, best fit with Prophet) and multivariate regression (predicting query latency from system state, best fit with gradient-boosted trees like XGBoost or LightGBM).
options: Use XGBoost for everything and never Prophet
Prophet for seasonal infrastructure metrics like CPU and connections; XGBoost/LightGBM for predicting query latency from multivariate system state
LSTM networks for all metrics regardless of data volume
Linear regression for query latency prediction
questions.q: Which model family does the chapter recommend for each forecasting problem?

questions.explain: The chapter warns that standard K-fold cross-validation leaks future data into training folds, producing optimistically biased metrics, and requires TimeSeriesSplit or walk-forward validation with the holdout as the most recent portion of history.
options: It is too slow for large datasets
It leaks future data into training folds, producing optimistically biased metrics
It requires labeled anomaly data
It cannot handle missing values
questions.q: Why is standard K-fold cross-validation invalid for database telemetry model validation?

questions.explain: The collector section states that cumulative counters are only useful as deltas between consecutive snapshots (e.g., delta of total_exec_ms_cumulative divided by 60 seconds), and that the service restart discontinuity in sys.dm_os_wait_stats must be handled explicitly.
options: Cumulative counters are only useful as deltas between consecutive snapshots, with explicit handling of the service restart discontinuity
Cumulative counters should be used raw as features
Cumulative counters should be ignored entirely
Cumulative counters must be multiplied by the snapshot interval
questions.q: How does the chapter recommend turning cumulative counters from sys.dm_exec_query_stats and sys.dm_os_wait_stats into ML features?

questions.explain: The chapter's minimum viable model lifecycle uses a rolling 7-day MAPE trigger: when it exceeds 1.5x the validation-time MAPE, an automated retraining job pulls the trailing 90 days and retrains; new models run 24-48h in shadow mode before promotion.
options: Retrain every hour regardless of error
Retrain only when a DBA manually requests it
When rolling 7-day MAPE exceeds 1.5x the validation-time MAPE, trigger automated retraining, then version and shadow-test the new model before promotion
Retrain once a year
questions.q: What drift-detection and retraining policy does the chapter define for production forecasting models?

questions.explain: The golden rule is that automated actions must be reversible, idempotent, and bounded: memory grant adjustments, read-traffic rerouting, pausing deferrable jobs, and statistics refreshes are automatable, while index changes, session kills, and global config changes require human approval.
options: Dropping indexes automatically
Killing long-running sessions without policy
Changing global configuration
Pausing non-critical deferrable SQL Server Agent jobs to clear headroom before a forecasted peak
questions.q: Which action does the chapter consider a defensible candidate for full automation in a prediction-action loop?
